content.p: On 30 March 2024, Veronica Butler, 27, and her friend Jilian Kelley, 39, set out from Hugoton, Kansas, to collect Butler's two children for a birthday party. They never arrived. Two weeks later, Oklahoma investigators dug their bodies out of a freezer that had been buried in a cattle pasture. Five people from the Oklahoma Panhandle were charged with kidnapping and murder, and prosecutors tied the killings to a custody dispute that had run for years.

One defendant, Tifany Adams, the children's grandmother and described by KFDA as the alleged ringleader, pleaded no contest in October 2025 and was sentenced on 2 February 2026 to two terms of life without parole. Two more defendants have plea agreements that require them to testify. The remaining two, Tad Cullum and Cole Twombly, have pleaded not guilty and are the subject of death-penalty filings. Everything said below about people who have not been convicted is an accusation, not a finding.
content.h2: A custody fight with a deadline
content.p: According to an affidavit by Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation Special Agent Jason Ott, Adams was in a "problematic custody battle" with Butler. Butler had two children with Adams's son, Wrangler Rickman. NBC News, citing the court record, reported that the dispute began in February 2019. Butler was allowed only supervised visits, every Saturday, and Kelley was authorised to supervise them. BBC News reported the children's ages as six and eight.

The affidavit said Rickman was in a rehabilitation facility in Oklahoma City when the women disappeared, and NBC reported that he did not appear to be a suspect. It also said that Adams at times kept the children and refused to hand them to Rickman even though he held legal custody.

A wrongful-death lawsuit filed in March 2025 by Butler's mother, Amanda Verner, gives a fuller version of the family history, and it is her allegation, not a court finding. The suit says Butler was awarded full custody in 2021, lost it the following year. The suit blames a false report by Adams that a relative of Butler's had sexually assaulted the children. Butler was left with limited supervised visits. It also alleges that Adams falsified records that helped her son win custody.

The timing matters to the prosecution's account. Butler's lawyer told investigators she was likely to get unsupervised visitation at a hearing on 17 April 2024. The affidavit alleged that Adams "vehemently opposed this and went to great lengths to plan and purchase items used in Butler and Kelley's murders."

Butler and Kelley were due to collect the children from Adams at about 10 a.m. and go to a birthday party. They were driving from Hugoton to Four Corners, Oklahoma, according to the affidavit. Their phones were still pinging carriers until roughly 9:42 a.m., then went silent. The phones have not been recovered, according to the probable cause documents.

When the women did not arrive, Butler's family found her vehicle abandoned in a rural part of Texas County near the Kansas line, and called the police. The Associated Press, as relayed by KWCH, put the spot on a rural highway about 11 miles south of Elkhart, Kansas. The probable cause documents say investigators found evidence of a severe injury: blood on the roadway, Butler's glasses south of the vehicle "near a broken hammer," and a pistol magazine inside Kelley's purse, though no pistol was found. Oklahoma authorities issued an endangered missing advisory on 30 March.
content.h2: What investigators say the planning looked like
content.p: The probable cause documents say state investigators extracted data from Adams's phone showing web searches for "taser pain level, gun shops, prepaid cellular phones and how to get someone out of their house." They allege she bought five stun guns and three prepaid phones in the months and days before the disappearance; NBC reported a Walmart purchase of the phones on 13 February. According to the affidavit, all three phones were near the place where Butler's car was found and at the women's last known location when they vanished.

A witness described in the documents is the 16-year-old daughter of Cora Twombly. Under the name "CW" she told investigators that on 29 March her mother and her mother's husband, Cole Twombly, said they would be gone the next morning on a "mission." The affidavit says they came home around noon and asked her to clean their pickup truck. According to the same document, Cora Twombly told her that things did not go as planned but that Butler would no longer be a worry for them. Cora Twombly allegedly said she and Cole had blocked the road to stop the women and deliver them to where Adams and Cullum were. These are statements recorded by an agent, not tested testimony.

The daughter also told investigators that there had been "other attempts to kill Butler" in February. BBC News, citing a teenage witness who spoke to investigators, described one alleged earlier plan: to throw an anvil through Butler's windshield "because anvils regularly fall off work vehicles."

The same witness described the group the defendants belonged to. The affidavit calls it "an anti-government group that had a religious affiliation" which called itself "God's Misfits" and met weekly, sometimes at the Twomblys' home.

Cell-phone data from two of the prepaid phones led investigators to a pasture rented by Cullum, where earth had been dug out and then put back, according to the affidavit as relayed by CNN's wire service. They excavated the soil and found two bodies, about 8.5 miles from where the car was found. A stun gun was found near the site. Cullum rented the land for cattle grazing, court records say, according to NBC.

Four people were arrested on Saturday 13 April 2024 in Texas and Cimarron Counties: Adams, then 54; Cullum, 43; Cole Twombly, 50; and Cora Twombly, 44. The booking charges for each were double murder, double kidnapping and a single conspiracy count. The remains were recovered on Sunday 14 April. The Oklahoma chief medical examiner confirmed their identities two days later. OSBI director Aungela Spurlock said: "This case did not end in the way that we had hoped." Sheriff Matt Boley said the attack was "targeted" rather than random.

A judge denied bail to all four on the Wednesday after the arrests. KWCH reported that a warrant was issued ten days later for a fifth suspect, Paul Jeremiah Grice, 31, and NBC reported that he was then charged. Per the arrest affidavit, Grice told an OSBI agent he took part in the killing and burial.

The Oklahoma Office of the Chief Medical Examiner released its summary in the autumn of 2024. KWCH reports it concluded that both women died from multiple sharp force trauma. NBC reported in November 2024 that Butler had 30 wounds, ten of them consistent with attempts to defend herself, plus a head laceration that may have been caused by a stun gun. The examiner's office said she was most likely dead when she was placed in the freezer. People, citing KVII, gave a breakdown of nine stab wounds and 21 other cuts. The two outlets break down the same autopsy differently.

Verner's lawsuit alleges the freezer sat in a hole about 12 feet deep packed with soil, cement, rocks and equipment. It says the women were hit with stun guns, abducted and taken to the pasture, and that the Twomblys' vehicle was used to block the road. All of these are allegations in a civil complaint.

A gag order was issued in May 2024 because of the amount of local and national coverage, according to KFDA's recap of the case. Preliminary hearings began in December 2024. Cora Twombly and Grice testified under plea agreements. KFDA, which obtained the transcript, reported that they described Adams recruiting them after telling them in graphic detail about abuse of Butler's children by a family member. The hearing papers, as KFDA summarised them, assign roles on the day: the Twomblys as lookouts, Grice and Cullum as the killers, and Adams as the person who cleaned up and supervised. Grice said he stabbed both women and cut his own hand, and that he felt Adams had set him up to take the blame. This is testimony from two co-defendants who had bargained for leniency, and the other defendants have not been convicted on the strength of it.

Grice testified that he would not face the death penalty in exchange. Cora Twombly's agreement includes testifying and serving 30 years before she can seek parole, according to KFDA and KWCH. KFDA also reported that all defendants waived the right to a speedy trial at the end of the pre-trial hearings.

Cullum separately asked for the trial judge to be removed on the ground that the judge had earlier represented Adams. The judge refused, and the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals also refused, according to KFDA. A temporary judge, Justin Eilers, was assigned to his case.

In October 2025, Adams entered no-contest pleas to nine charges: for each of the two women, murder, moving a body, desecrating a corpse and child neglect, plus one conspiracy count. News 9 described a no-contest plea as accepting the conviction without admitting guilt. KFDA reported that she accepted responsibility and would serve the rest of her life in prison. Fox News, citing court documents, reported that the state agreed not to seek the death penalty against her.

On 2 February 2026 a Texas County judge sentenced her to life without the possibility of parole on each murder count, plus five years on each body-removal count and seven years on each corpse-desecration count. News 9 reported that the sentences run concurrently. People gave her age as 56 at sentencing; NBC and other outlets gave it as 54 at the time of her arrest.
content.h2: The two men still facing trial
content.p: In October 2025 prosecutors filed a bill of particulars saying they would seek death sentences for Cullum and Cole Twombly. The state alleged that the defendants put more than one person at great risk of death, that the murders were "especially heinous, atrocious, or cruel," and that Kelley's murder was committed to avoid arrest or prosecution. Prosecutors also alleged a probability that each man would commit violent acts that would threaten society. An amended filing against Cullum, covered by KFDA in March 2026, lists five statutory aggravating circumstances and asks that he be sentenced to death on both counts.

At an arraignment on 5 November 2025 Cullum pleaded not guilty. Twombly stood mute and the court entered a not-guilty plea for him. Fox News listed their charges as two murder counts, conspiracy, removal of a body and desecration of a corpse.

The trial dates have moved. In late 2025 Cullum's trial was set for 1 June 2026 and Twombly's for 19 October 2026. On 23 January 2026 the judge postponed both. KFDA reported the new dates as 16 October for Cullum and February 2027 for Twombly (KVII gave Cullum's as 19 October), and said the court wanted to ensure due process and a fair trial. The judge also denied Cullum's motion to dismiss, saying there was sufficient evidence at the preliminary examination. Cullum's lawyers have filed more than 30 motions, including one asking the court to declare the death penalty unconstitutional as cruel and unusual punishment.
In February 2026, KWCH still gave 16 October 2026 as the date of Cullum's trial.

Cora Twombly and Grice have plea agreements and were described by KFDA in October 2025 as awaiting sentencing. KFDA said in November 2025 that they were due back in court in August 2026. Cullum and Cole Twombly are presumed innocent unless a jury decides otherwise.

Wrangler Rickman, who held custody of the children, was reported by NBC not to appear to be a suspect and was not charged. Butler's mother asked the community, after a November 2025 hearing, to pray for "redemption, forgiveness, and salvation for everyone involved," according to Fox News's report of her remarks to KSN. Garrett R. Oates, a lawyer who had represented Butler, said the case "highlights the conflict, stress, and magnitude of decisions that go into any child custody case."
